clips.title: Python in 100 Seconds
clips.why: A fast first look at what Python code looks like, before we compare it with TypeScript line by line.
look: How a block is marked: by indentation, not by braces.
How a variable is created: a name and a value, with no let or const.
How a function is written with def.
clips.after: Every Python file in fcp's backend and in the eval bench uses these same few shapes, so after this clip most of a diff reads like TypeScript with different punctuation.

clips.title: Python Tutorial: Type Hinting vs Type Checking vs Data Validation - What’s the Difference?
clips.why: Corey Schafer separates the three ideas this lesson is about: writing a type hint, checking hints with a separate tool, and validating data when the program runs.
look: Python runs the code even when a value does not match its hint.
A type checker is a separate tool that reads the hints before the code runs, the job tsc does for TypeScript.
What the hints give you even when no checker runs.
clips.after: fcp's backend uses hints but runs no type checker in CI, so the tests and your review are the check, exactly the gap the 0% story fell into.

clips.title: Python Tutorial: UV - A Faster, All-in-One Package Manager to Replace Pip and Venv
clips.why: The same speaker creates a project with uv, so you see pyproject.toml, the lockfile and .venv appear one after the other.
look: uv init writes pyproject.toml: compare it with a package.json in your head.
When .venv and uv.lock appear, and which command created them.
Where the packages end up: inside the project folder, not on the whole laptop.
clips.after: fcp's backend is set up the same way: a pyproject.toml with requires-python 3.13, a committed uv.lock, and CI that runs uv sync --frozen.

practice.q: Which Python line does the same as const failed = rewards.filter(r => r === 0);?

options.text: failed = [r for r in rewards if r == 0]
options.why: A list comprehension is filter (and map) in one expression, and == compares values the way === does.
Python has no const, and lists have no .filter method. The comprehension is the usual way.

options.text: failed = [r for r in rewards if r === 0]
options.why: Python has no ===. Its == already compares without converting types, so "0" == 0 is False.

practice.q: Finish the line so a string read from a file becomes a number before it goes into the Trial.
practice.why: The field's type is only a hint, so nothing converts the string for you. int(reward) turns "1" into 1 where the data enters the program.

practice.q: A pull request adds a function with careful type hints and a test that never calls it with a wrong type. In fcp, what checks that callers respect those hints?

options.text: Python itself, when the function is called.
options.why: Python stores hints and ignores them at run time.
fcp's flake8 reports only real errors such as undefined names and unused imports, never types.

options.text: Nothing automatic: only tests that call it the way real callers do, and your review.
options.why: fcp runs no type checker in CI, so hints are documentation. Tests and reviewers are what turn them into facts.

practice.q: The script has no type checker yet. Add mypy as a development-only dependency, the way npm install -D mypy would.
practice.hint: The same idea as a devDependency.
practice.why: uv add --dev writes mypy into the dev dependency group in pyproject.toml and pins it in uv.lock, so the script does not need it to run.

practice.q: You clone a Python project that uses uv and want to run its tests. Put the steps in order.
items: Read requires-python in pyproject.toml to see which Python it needs
Run uv sync --frozen, which creates .venv and installs exactly what uv.lock says
Run the tests through uv run pytest, so they use the project's .venv
If an import fails with ModuleNotFoundError, check that you ran through uv run before installing anything
practice.why: The project file says what is needed, the lockfile decides the exact versions, and uv run makes every command use that environment instead of your laptop's own Python.

practice.q: def failed_tasks(lines: list[str], seen: list[str] = []) is called on Monday and again on Tuesday. Why does Tuesday's answer still contain Monday's failures?

options.text: The default list is created once, when def runs, and every call shares it.
options.why: Unlike TypeScript, Python evaluates a default value one time. Use None as the default and create the list inside the function.

options.text: Python caches the result of a function that is called with the same arguments.
options.why: Python caches nothing by itself. The list grows because both calls append to the same object.

options.text: The type hint list[str] makes the list global.
options.why: Hints change nothing at run time. The shared default value is the cause.
